blocks.text: 1. RAG Workflow

blocks.alt: A query is embedded, searched, assembled, then generated

blocks.text: RAG Architecture closed by pointing here. RAG Workflow traces one real request through that architecture from start to finish.
It walks through a single query, step by step, from arrival to final answer.
2. Recapping The Preview
RAG workflow was previewed in that earlier topic as walking through how a query flows through the architecture.
This topic walks through that flow in full, step by step.
3. Recapping The Offline Versus Online Split
Ingestion, chunking, embedding, and indexing, all covered in RAG Architecture, happen offline, before any query.
Retrieval and generation happen online instead, every time a query actually arrives, and that is the key distinction this workflow builds on.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Phase","What happens"],"rows":[["Offline","Ingestion, chunking, embedding, indexing"],["Online","Retrieval and generation, on every live query"]]}

blocks.text: 4. Step One: Query Arrives
The workflow begins the moment a real, live query arrives from a user.
Everything from this point forward happens in the online, query-time path.
5. Step Two: Query Embedding

blocks.alt: A query is embedded into a query vector

blocks.text: The raw query text gets converted into an embedding, using the technique covered in Embeddings.
This step uses the exact same embedding model that was used during offline indexing.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This consistency requirement explains why query and chunk embeddings must come from the exact same model: otherwise their vectors would not be comparable at all.

blocks.text: 6. Step Three: Similarity Search

blocks.alt: A query vector searches the vector index to produce top-k results

blocks.text: That query embedding then gets compared against every stored chunk embedding in the index.
Using cosine similarity, the technique covered in Sentence Embeddings, this returns the most similar matches.
7. Step Four: Context Assembly

blocks.alt: Top-k chunks are assembled into context

blocks.text: The retrieved chunks then get assembled together into one combined block of context.
That assembly gets a full, dedicated treatment later, in Context Management.
8. Step Five: Prompt Construction

blocks.alt: Context and query combine into a final prompt

blocks.text: That assembled context then gets combined with the original query into one final prompt.
Using the prompting techniques covered earlier, this follows a consistent, repeatable template.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Workflow step","Input consumed"],"rows":[["Context assembly","Retrieved chunks from the similarity search"],["Prompt construction","Assembled context plus the original query"]]}

blocks.text: 9. Step Six: Generation

blocks.alt: A prompt goes through an LLM to produce a response

blocks.text: The language model then generates its answer, using the next token prediction mechanism covered in Next Token Prediction.
It works one token at a time, conditioned on the fully assembled prompt, the sixth and final step in the workflow.
10. Recognizing Why Tracing The Full Workflow Matters For Debugging
Tracing the full workflow helps pinpoint exactly where a bad answer actually went wrong.
A well tested, stable pipeline, the kind described in RAG Architecture, needs less step by step tracing.
11. Worked Example
The example below demonstrates all six workflow steps executed in sequence for one query.

code.content:
def simple_embed(text):
    return [len(text), text.lower().count("o")]

indexed_chunks = [
    ("The office reopens on Monday.", simple_embed("The office reopens on Monday.")),
    ("Parking is available on level two.", simple_embed("Parking is available on level two.")),
]

# step one: the query arrives
query = "When does the office reopen?"

# step two: query embedding
query_embedding = simple_embed(query)

# step three: similarity search
scored = [(chunk, sum((a - b) ** 2 for a, b in zip(query_embedding, emb)) ** 0.5) for chunk, emb in indexed_chunks]
scored.sort(key=lambda item: item[1])
top_chunk = scored[0][0]

# step four: context assembly
assembled_context = top_chunk

# step five: prompt construction
final_prompt = f"Context: {assembled_context}\nQuestion: {query}\nAnswer:"

# step six: generation
def generate(prompt):
    return "The office reopens on Monday, based on the retrieved context."

print(f"Query: {query}")
print(f"Retrieved chunk: {top_chunk}")
print(f"Final prompt:\n{final_prompt}")
print(f"\nGenerated answer: {generate(final_prompt)}")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example shows all six workflow steps executing in sequence for one query, from arrival through embedding, retrieval, assembly, prompting, and finally generation.

blocks.text: 12. Common Mistakes

items: Confusing which steps happen offline during ingestion versus online at query time.
Using a different embedding model for the query than the one used for indexed chunks.
Skipping context assembly and passing raw, unstructured retrieved chunks directly to the model.
Not tracing intermediate steps when debugging a bad answer, jumping straight to blaming generation.

blocks.text: 13. Key Takeaways

items: RAG workflow traces one real query from arrival to final answer, step by step.
Ingestion, chunking, embedding, and indexing happen offline; retrieval and generation happen online.
The workflow begins the moment a real query arrives, starting the online, query-time path.
The query gets embedded using the exact same model already used for indexing.
That embedding gets compared against every stored chunk to find the most similar matches.
Retrieved chunks get assembled into one combined block of context.
That context combines with the original query into one final, structured prompt.
The language model generates its answer one token at a time from that assembled prompt.
